title: Framework Demo
description: One question of every type, used to exercise the engine and as a copy-paste reference for bank authors.

market.title: A simple market
market.body: Market demand is **Q<sub>d</sub> = 140 − 2P** and market supply is **Q<sub>s</sub> = P + 5**.

table.caption: Table D-1 · Hours needed to make one unit

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. In a perfectly competitive equilibrium, what are the price and quantity traded?
options: price will be $20 and quantity will be 25
price will be $45 and quantity will be 50
price will be $35 and quantity will be 40
price will be $10 and quantity will be 15
questions.explanation: Set Q<sub>d</sub> = Q<sub>s</sub>: 140 − 2P = P + 5 → 135 = 3P → **P = 45**. Substitute back: Q = 45 + 5 = **50**.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. If the market price were $60, what would the size of the surplus be (in units)?
Which of the following would shift the demand curve for coffee to the **right**? Select all that apply.
options: An increase in consumer income (coffee is a normal good)
A fall in the price of tea, a substitute
A fall in the price of coffee creamer, a complement
A fall in the price of coffee itself
questions.explanation: Income up (normal good) and a cheaper complement both raise demand at every price. A cheaper *substitute* pulls buyers away (demand falls). A change in coffee's own price is a **movement along** the curve, not a shift.

questions.prompt: A price ceiling set *above* the equilibrium price is binding and creates a shortage.
questions.explanation: A ceiling only binds when it is set **below** P*. Above P* the market simply settles at equilibrium and the ceiling has no effect.

figure.caption: Figure D-1 · Production possibilities for food and machines

questions.prompt: Refer to Figure D-1. What is the opportunity cost of moving from point D to point A?
questions.explanation: D → A gives up 60 − 30 = 30 machines to gain 30 − 10 = 20 food. Per unit of food: 30 ÷ 20 = **3/2 machine**.

questions.prompt: Consumer incomes rise and coffee is a **normal good**. Draw the new demand curve **D₂** and mark the new equilibrium **E₂**.

tasks.label: D₂
tasks.prompt: Draw the new demand curve D₂

questions.explanation: Higher income raises the demand for a normal good at **every** price, so the whole curve shifts right. Supply is unchanged, so the market slides up along S: both equilibrium price and quantity rise.

questions.prompt: The supply curve is P = 20 + 3Q. Mark the point on the supply curve showing quantity supplied when the price is **$110**.

tasks.label: Q at $110
tasks.prompt: Place the point on S where P = $110

questions.explanation: Solve 110 = 20 + 3Q → Q = **30**. A change in the good's own price is a movement *along* the supply curve — supply itself does not shift.

questions.prompt: The government imposes a binding **price ceiling**. Draw the ceiling as a horizontal line below the equilibrium price, then mark the quantity supplied at that price on the supply curve.

hints.shift: A binding ceiling must sit below the equilibrium price.

tasks.label: Qₛ
tasks.prompt: Mark quantity supplied at the ceiling

questions.explanation: A binding ceiling is a horizontal line **below** P*. At that lower price, producers move down along S and supply less (Q<sub>s</sub> < Q*), while consumers want more (Q<sub>d</sub> > Q*) — a shortage.
